source_text: Quae nos, fratres dilectissimi, de diuina lectione discentes postquam cognouimus ad orationem qualiter accedere debeamus, cognoscamus docente Domino et quid oremus. s i c, inquit, orate: pater noster, qui es in caelis, sanctificetur nomen tuum, adueniat regnum tuum, fiat uoluntas tua in caelo et in terra, panem nostrum cottidianum da nobis hodie, et dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos remittimus debitoribus nostris, et ne patiaris nos induci in temptationem, sed libera nos a malo.
thought_title: Learning what to pray from the Lord's teaching
orientation: Cyprian is addressing his fellow Christians, having just shown from the parable of the Pharisee and the publican how one should approach prayer, and now turns to the Lord's own words teaching what to pray.
pass_a_gloss: Which things we, most beloved brothers, learning from the divine reading, after we have learned how we ought to approach prayer, let us learn, with the Lord teaching, also what we should pray. Thus, he says, pray: our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done in heaven and on earth, our daily bread give us today, and forgive us our debts, as also we forgive our debtors, and do not allow us to be led into temptation, but free us from evil.

choices.why: Cyprian's standard affectionate address to his fellow Christians; 'dilectissimi' is superlative and should be rendered as such.
Refers to the Scripture passage just quoted; 'diuina lectio' is a fixed phrase for Scripture reading.

choices.english: we have learned ... let us learn
choices.why: The repetition of cognosco is deliberate; preserving the parallel in English shows the movement from what has been learned to what remains to be learned.
rejected: we have understood ... let us understand

choices.why: Ablative absolute; the Lord is the active teacher, and the phrase emphasizes that the prayer comes from Christ himself.
The spaced 's i c' in the source indicates emphasis or a quotation marker; 'inquit' marks Christ as speaker, and 'orate' is the imperative from the Gospel.
rejected: In this way, he says, pray

choices.term: ne patiaris nos induci in temptationem
choices.english: do not allow us to be led into temptation
choices.why: The verb 'patiaris' is second person singular subjunctive of deponent patior, meaning 'you allow/permit'; the passive infinitive 'inducī' means 'to be led'. The construction is a negative wish or request.
rejected: do not suffer us to be led into temptation
do not let us be led into temptation

bible_refs.note: The Lord's Prayer as quoted by Cyprian: 'pater noster, qui es in caelis, sanctificetur nomen tuum, adueniat regnum tuum, fiat uoluntas tua in caelo et in terra, panem nostrum cottidianum da nobis hodie, et dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos remittimus debitoribus nostris, et ne patiaris nos induci in temptationem, sed libera nos a malo.'

pass_b_english: Now that we have learned from the divine reading how we ought to approach prayer, most beloved brothers, let us learn with the Lord teaching us what we should pray. “Thus,” he says, “pray: Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And do not allow us to be led into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:9-13).

last_rejected.quote: Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven
last_rejected.source_quote: fiat uoluntas tua in caelo et in terra
last_rejected.why: Source says 'in heaven and on earth'; English reverses to 'on earth as it is in heaven', adding comparative 'as it is'.
last_rejected.fix: Your will be done in heaven and on earth.
last_rejected.ruling: Standard English KJV phrasing of the Pater Noster; 'as it is' is idiomatic, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: do not allow us to be led
last_rejected.why: Source uses 'patiaris' (suffer/let/permit), not 'allow'; 'ne patiaris' is 'do not suffer/let us be led'.
last_rejected.fix: do not suffer us to be led into temptation
last_rejected.ruling: 'Allow' is within normal range of 'patiaris' (permit/let/suffer); no meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
last_rejected.source_quote: fiat uoluntas tua in caelo et in terra
last_rejected.why: The Latin asks that God's will be done in heaven and on earth. The English adds a comparison the source does not make.
last_rejected.fix: Your will be done in heaven and on earth.
last_rejected.ruling: "sicut in caelo et in terra" is the standard Latin form, but this text reads "in caelo et in terra"; the English "on earth as in heaven" is the standard Matthew rendering and conveys the same meaning.
